finding.claim: SQL injection in /search: the q parameter is interpolated into the SQL string with an f-string, so an attacker can alter the query. They can use UNION SELECT to read any table in shop.db, or a boolean or error-based approach to extract data. sqlite3's execute() rejects multiple statements, so stacked-query writes are not possible.
finding.source: request.args.get('q') on the unauthenticated GET /search endpoint (app.py:11)
finding.sink: db.execute(f"SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%{term}%'") (app.py:12)

trace.note: Route /search is registered with no authentication decorator
term = request.args.get('q', '') takes attacker-controlled input with no validation
term is placed inside the LIKE literal with an f-string; a payload such as %' UNION SELECT id, name FROM sqlite_master-- breaks out of the quotes
Query results are returned to the caller via jsonify, so extracted data is reflected in the response

finding.guards_checked: No parameterization on this path. The other queries (app.py:18, 25) use ? placeholders, but this one does not. No input validation or escaping, no allowlist, no WAF or middleware, and no authentication or authorization on the route. Flask has no global sanitizer. The sqlite3 module blocks stacked statements, which limits the impact to data disclosure and does not remove it.

verdict.reason: app.py:11-12 puts the unauthenticated request.args 'q' value into an f-string SQL LIKE literal with no parameterization, validation or auth (app.py:9), and app.py:13 returns the rows via jsonify, so UNION-based data disclosure works.
